implementation_notes: Rails ships the endpoint: GET /up is routed to Rails::HealthController#show, which returns 200 when the application booted without exceptions and 500 otherwise, and the route can be remapped (get "healthz" => "rails/health#show"). The documentation is explicit that this check deliberately does not reflect dependencies such as the database or Redis and that applications with specific needs should replace it with their own controller action - which is precisely the liveness/readiness split: keep /up (or a remapped equivalent) as the liveness signal and add a small action that checks the instance-local resources the application really needs, with a timeout. Outside Rails the same thing is a Rack middleware or a Sinatra route returning a three-element response.
idiom_name: Rails::HealthController at /up (plus a custom readiness action)
code_sketch:
# config/routes.rb
Rails.application.routes.draw do
  get "up" => "rails/health#show", as: :rails_health_check    # liveness: app booted
  get "healthz/ready" => "health#ready"                      # readiness: dependencies
end

class HealthController < ApplicationController
  def ready
    ActiveRecord::Base.connection.select_value("SELECT 1")
    render plain: "ok"
  rescue ActiveRecord::ActiveRecordError, Redis::CannotConnectError
    render plain: "not ready", status: :service_unavailable
  end
end
pitfalls: /up answers 200 as long as the process booted, so using it as a readiness probe routes traffic to an instance whose database connection is gone - the framework documents this limitation rather than hiding it.

A readiness action that runs a real query on every poll competes for connections with traffic; use the cheapest sufficient check (SELECT 1, a connection-pool probe) and keep it out of the request-serving connection pool where the adapter allows.

A health action that inherits ApplicationController drags in filters and middleware (authentication, locale, request tracking); an orchestrator that cannot satisfy them receives a redirect or 401 instead of a status.
